skills.cond-mult: Multiplication rule, trees and total probability
skills.dl-lln: Law of large numbers and inequalities

items.title: Choosing a portfolio
items.prose: A fund manager picks 3 of 10 stocks for a new portfolio. The order of picking does not matter.
items.question: How many different portfolios are possible?

options.why: You counted ordered picks, so each portfolio appears 6 times.
You multiplied 10 by 3, which does not count choices.
You allowed repeats and counted order.

feedback.correct: Ordered picks, divided by the orders of the same three stocks.
feedback.generic: Count ordered picks, then divide by the number of orders of three stocks.

explain.text: There are $10 \cdot 9 \cdot 8 = 720$ ordered picks. Each set of three appears in $3! = 6$ orders, so there are $\tbinom{10}{3} = 120$ portfolios.

items.title: A small total
items.prose: Two fair dice are rolled. The grid shows every outcome with its total.
items.question: How many outcomes have a total of at most 4?

feedback.correct: Six cells in the corner have a total of 4 or less.
feedback.generic: Count cells, and treat (1, 2) and (2, 1) as different outcomes.

byKey.unordered: You counted unordered pairs. (1, 2) and (2, 1) are different cells of the table.

explain.text: The outcomes are (1, 1), (1, 2), (2, 1), (1, 3), (2, 2) and (3, 1). That is 6 of the 36 cells.

items.title: At least one six in four rolls
items.prose: Four fair dice are rolled.
items.question: What is the chance at least one shows a 6? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.correct: The complement, no sixes at all, is the easy event.
feedback.generic: Find the chance of no 6 at all, then use the complement.

byKey.added: You added $\tfrac{1}{6}$ four times. That counts rolls with two sixes more than once.
byKey.none: You found the chance of no 6 at all. Subtract it from 1.

explain.text: No 6 on any of four dice has chance $\left(\tfrac{5}{6}\right)^4 = \tfrac{625}{1296}$. The complement is $1 - \tfrac{625}{1296} = \tfrac{671}{1296} \approx 0.5177$.

items.title: Given a total of 4
items.prose: Two fair dice are rolled. You learn the total is 4.
items.question: What is the chance the first die shows 1?

options.why: You ignored the news about the total.
You compared (1, 3) with (3, 1) and left out (2, 2).
You divided by the whole table instead of the three cells left.

feedback.correct: Three outcomes are left and one starts with 1.
feedback.generic: List the outcomes with a total of 4.

explain.text: A total of 4 leaves (1, 3), (2, 2) and (3, 1). One of the three starts with 1, so the chance is $\tfrac{1}{3}$.

items.title: At least one six
items.prose: You roll two fair dice out of sight. A friend who can see them says at least one of them is a 6.
items.question: What is the chance both dice show 6?

options.why: You treated the news as being about one named die. Your friend checked both.
You ignored what your friend told you.
You counted (6, 6) twice when listing the outcomes with a 6.

feedback.correct: Eleven outcomes have a 6, and one of them is a double six.
feedback.generic: Count the outcomes with at least one 6 without double counting.

explain.text: All 36 outcomes minus the 25 with no 6 leaves 11. Only (6, 6) has both dice on 6, so the chance is $\tfrac{1}{11}$.

items.title: Second counter red
items.prose: A bag holds 3 red and 2 blue counters. You draw two, one after the other, without replacement.
items.question: Given that the second counter is red, what is the chance the first was red?

options.why: You ignored the condition. A red second counter uses up one of the reds.
That is the chance the first was blue.
That is $P(R_1 \cap R_2)$. Divide it by $P(R_2)$.

feedback.correct: Divide the chance of two reds by the chance of a red second counter.
feedback.generic: Use the definition: the joint chance over the chance of the condition.

explain.text: Two reds has chance $\tfrac{3}{5} \cdot \tfrac{2}{4} = \tfrac{3}{10}$. By symmetry the second counter is red with chance $\tfrac{3}{5}$. So $P(R_1 \mid R_2) = \tfrac{3/10}{3/5} = \tfrac{1}{2}$.

items.title: A positive test
items.prose: A screening test is used where 1% of people have a condition. It detects 95% of cases and wrongly flags 10% of healthy people.
items.question: A person tests positive. What is the chance they have the condition? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: Most positives come from the large healthy group.
feedback.generic: Find the chance of a positive test first, by adding both routes to it.

byKey.sensitivity: You gave $P(+ \mid D)$. The question asks for $P(D \mid +)$, the condition turned round.
byKey.joint: You gave $P(D \cap +)$. Divide it by the chance of a positive test.
byKey.specificity: You gave the chance a healthy person tests negative.

explain.text: A positive has chance $0.95 \times 0.01 + 0.10 \times 0.99 = 0.1085$. Bayes’ rule gives $\tfrac{0.0095}{0.1085} \approx 0.0876$. In 10,000 people that is 95 true positives against 990 false ones.

items.title: Which pairs are independent
items.prose: Two fair dice are rolled. $A$ is the first die is even, $B$ is the total is 7 and $C$ is the total is 8.
items.question: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.why: $P(A \cap C) = \tfrac{3}{36}$, but $P(A)\,P(C) = \tfrac{5}{72}$.
They cannot both happen, so learning one rules out the other.

feedback.correct: Only the first die and a total of 7 multiply exactly.
feedback.generic: Test each pair: does the joint chance equal the product?

explain.text: $P(A \cap B) = \tfrac{3}{36} = \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot \tfrac{1}{6}$, so $A$ and $B$ are independent. $P(A \cap C) = \tfrac{3}{36}$ but $P(A)P(C) = \tfrac{5}{72}$. Disjoint events with positive chances are never independent.

items.title: After six heads
items.prose: A fair coin has landed heads six times in a row.
items.question: What is the chance the next toss lands heads?

options.why: You expected tails to be due. The coin has no memory of past tosses.
You read the run as a hot streak. A fair coin does not warm up.
That is the chance of seven heads in a row before any toss. Six have already happened.

feedback.correct: Tosses are independent, so the run changes nothing.
feedback.generic: Ask whether the next toss depends on the earlier ones.

explain.text: Each toss of a fair coin is independent of the others. The chance of heads on the next toss is $\tfrac{1}{2}$, whatever came before.

items.title: Heads in three tosses
items.prose: $X$ is the number of heads in three tosses of a fair coin.
items.question: Fill in the two missing probabilities.

feedback.correct: Three of the eight outcomes give each middle value.
feedback.generic: Count the outcomes with exactly one head, then exactly two.

explain.text: One head happens in HTT, THT and TTH, so $P(X = 1) = \tfrac{3}{8} = 0.375$. Two heads also has three outcomes, so $P(X = 2) = 0.375$.

items.title: A bet on a die
items.prose: You pay £4 to roll a fair die and receive the number shown in pounds.
items.question: What is your expected profit per bet, in pounds?

feedback.correct: The payout averages 3.5, so you lose 50p a bet on average.
feedback.generic: Find the average payout, then subtract the price.

byKey.gross: You gave the average payout. Profit subtracts the £4 you paid.

explain.text: The payout has mean $\tfrac{1 + 2 + \dots + 6}{6} = 3.5$. Subtract the £4 price: the expected profit is $-0.5$.

items.title: Neighbouring heads
items.prose: You flip a fair coin 10 times. A double is a pair of neighbouring flips that are both heads, so HHH holds two doubles.
items.question: What is the expected number of doubles?

feedback.correct: Nine pairs, each a double with chance one quarter.
feedback.generic: Use one indicator for each neighbouring pair and add their means.

byKey.ten-pairs: You used 10 pairs. Ten flips have only 9 neighbouring pairs.
byKey.heads: You gave the expected number of heads, not of doubles.

explain.text: Let $I_k = 1$ when flips $k$ and $k + 1$ are both heads, so $E[I_k] = \tfrac{1}{4}$. Linearity holds even for dependent indicators, so the mean is $9 \cdot \tfrac{1}{4} = 2.25$.

items.title: Variance of a difference
items.prose: $X$ and $Y$ are independent, with $\mathrm{Var}(X) = 4$ and $\mathrm{Var}(Y) = 9$.
items.question: What is $\mathrm{Var}(2X - Y)$?

options.why: You subtracted the variances. The minus sign is squared, so they add.
You doubled $\mathrm{Var}(X)$. A constant comes out squared, so it is multiplied by 4.
A variance can never be negative.

feedback.correct: Constants come out squared, and independent variances add.
feedback.generic: Use $\mathrm{Var}(aX + bY) = a^2 \mathrm{Var}(X) + b^2 \mathrm{Var}(Y)$ for independent variables.

explain.text: Independence removes the covariance term. So $\mathrm{Var}(2X - Y) = 2^2 \cdot 4 + (-1)^2 \cdot 9 = 16 + 9 = 25$.

items.title: From a joint table
items.prose: The table gives the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$.
items.question: What is $P(Y = 1 \mid X = 1)$? Give a fraction or a decimal.

feedback.correct: Work inside the row where $X = 1$.
feedback.generic: Divide the joint probability by the row total.

byKey.joint: You gave $P(X = 1, Y = 1)$. Divide it by $P(X = 1)$.
byKey.marginal: You gave $P(Y = 1)$ over both rows. The condition keeps only the second row.

explain.text: The row $X = 1$ has total $0.2 + 0.4 = 0.6$. So $P(Y = 1 \mid X = 1) = \tfrac{0.4}{0.6} = \tfrac{2}{3}$.

items.title: A die, then coins
items.prose: You roll a fair die, then flip that many fair coins.
items.question: What is the expected number of heads?

feedback.correct: Given the roll $n$, the mean is $\tfrac{n}{2}$; then average over the roll.
feedback.generic: Condition on the die roll first, then average.

byKey.no-half: You gave the mean number of coins. Each coin is heads only half the time.
byKey.one-coin: You gave the mean for one coin. The die decides how many coins there are.

explain.text: Given the die shows $N$, the expected number of heads is $\tfrac{N}{2}$. Averaging over the roll gives $E\left[\tfrac{N}{2}\right] = \tfrac{3.5}{2} = 1.75$.

items.title: Three winning days of five
items.prose: A strategy makes money on 60% of days, independently from day to day.
items.question: Over 5 trading days, what is the chance it makes money on exactly 3? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: Choose the winning days, then multiply.
feedback.generic: This is a binomial count: choose which days win.

byKey.no-choose: You left out $\tbinom{5}{3} = 10$, the number of ways to pick the winning days.
byKey.one-day: That is the chance for one day, not three of five.

explain.text: The count is binomial with $n = 5$ and $p = 0.6$. So $P(X = 3) = \tbinom{5}{3}(0.6)^3(0.4)^2 = 10 \times 0.216 \times 0.16 = 0.3456$.

items.title: Waiting for a six
items.prose: You roll a fair die until the first 6 appears.
items.question: What is the expected number of rolls, counting the roll that shows the 6?

options.why: You counted the rolls before the 6, not the 6 itself.
That is the mean of a single roll.
That is the number of outcomes for two dice.

feedback.correct: A geometric count has mean one over the chance of success.
feedback.generic: Each roll succeeds with chance one sixth. How long is the wait on average?

explain.text: The number of rolls is geometric with $p = \tfrac{1}{6}$. Its mean is $\tfrac{1}{p} = 6$.

items.title: A uniform waiting time
items.prose: A delay $X$ is uniform between 0 and 10 seconds. The shaded area is $P(2 < X < 5)$.
items.question: What is $P(2 < X < 5)$?

feedback.correct: The interval covers three tenths of the range.
feedback.generic: For a uniform variable, probability is length over the whole range.

byKey.length: You gave the length of the interval. Divide it by the length of the whole range, 10.

explain.text: The density is $\tfrac{1}{10}$ on $[0, 10]$. The area over $(2, 5)$ is $3 \times \tfrac{1}{10} = 0.3$.

items.title: A normal tail
items.prose: $X$ is normal with mean 100 and standard deviation 15. Use $\Phi(2) = 0.9772$.
items.question: What is $P(X > 130)$?

options.why: You used the two-sided 5% cut-off. Here $z = 2$ and only one tail counts.
You used one standard deviation. 130 is two above the mean.
That is the area between the mean and $z = 2$.

feedback.correct: Standardise: 130 is two standard deviations above the mean.
feedback.generic: Find $z$ first, then the area beyond it.

items.title: What Chebyshev guarantees
items.prose: $X$ has mean 50 and standard deviation 5. Nothing else is known about its distribution.
items.question: What does Chebyshev’s inequality say about $P(|X - 50| \ge 15)$?

options.why: You divided by $k = 3$. The bound is $\tfrac{1}{k^2}$.
Chebyshev gives a bound, not the value.
That bound is for staying within 15 of the mean, the other event.

feedback.correct: 15 is three standard deviations, so the bound is one ninth.
feedback.generic: Write 15 as $k$ standard deviations, then use $\tfrac{1}{k^2}$.

explain.text: Here $15 = 3\sigma$, so $k = 3$. Chebyshev gives $P(|X - \mu| \ge k\sigma) \le \tfrac{1}{k^2} = \tfrac{1}{9}$, whatever the distribution.

items.title: A losing quarter
items.prose: A strategy’s daily P&L has mean £20 and standard deviation £100, independent across days. Use $\Phi(2) = 0.9772$.
items.question: Over 100 days, about what is the chance the total P&L is negative? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: The total has mean 2,000 and standard deviation 1,000.
feedback.generic: Find the mean and standard deviation of the total, then standardise 0.

byKey.linear-sd: You multiplied the standard deviation by 100. Variances add, so it grows by $\sqrt{100} = 10$.
byKey.unscaled: You kept a standard deviation of 100 for the total. It grows with the square root of the days.

explain.text: The total has mean $100 \times 20 = 2000$ and standard deviation $100\sqrt{100} = 1000$. By the central limit theorem, $P(S < 0) \approx \Phi(-2) = 0.0228$.

items.title: Two days in a regime chain
items.prose: A market switches between Calm and Volatile once a day, with the transition chances shown.
items.question: Today is Calm. What is the chance the market is Volatile two days from now? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: Two paths reach Volatile, and their chances add.
feedback.generic: List the two-day paths from Calm that end in Volatile.

byKey.one-step: That is one day ahead. The question asks for two.
byKey.one-path: You counted only the path that switches on the first day.
byKey.other-path: You counted only the path that switches on the second day.

explain.text: Calm, Calm, Volatile has chance $0.9 \times 0.1 = 0.09$. Calm, Volatile, Volatile has $0.1 \times 0.7 = 0.07$. Their sum, $0.16$, is the (Calm, Volatile) entry of $\mathbf{P}^2$.

items.title: The long run
items.prose: The same chain runs for many years.
items.question: In the long run, what share of days is Volatile? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: Flow out of Calm balances flow back into it.
feedback.generic: Set the flow from Calm to Volatile equal to the flow back.

byKey.half: Two states do not mean equal shares. The chain leaves Calm far less often.
byKey.one-step: That is the chance of switching from Calm in one day.

explain.text: In balance, $\pi_C \times 0.1 = \pi_V \times 0.3$ and $\pi_C + \pi_V = 1$. So $\pi_V = \tfrac{0.1}{0.1 + 0.3} = 0.25$.

items.title: How long the game lasts
items.prose: You start with £2 and bet £1 on each toss of a fair coin. You stop when you reach £5 or £0.
items.question: What is the expected number of tosses?

feedback.correct: First-step analysis gives $D_i = i(5 - i)$ tosses from £$i$.
feedback.generic: Let $D_i$ be the expected number of tosses from £$i$, and write one equation per state.

byKey.straight-up: You counted the three steps straight up to £5. The walk wanders, so it takes longer.
byKey.product: You multiplied the start by the target. The formula is $D_i = i(N - i)$.

explain.text: First-step analysis gives $D_i = 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}D_{i+1} + \tfrac{1}{2}D_{i-1}$ with $D_0 = D_5 = 0$. The solution is $D_i = i(5 - i)$, so $D_2 = 6$.
